# Volume 2 — XIV A Danger Averted

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

Mrs. Sowerby, burdened as always with every concern of church and state, caught up with Nell as she walked back from the post office on a Friday evening.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0000 }

“I’ve just visited Timothy Cotton’s place to find out if Alice Louise could assist me for a couple of days,” she stated. “I employed her last week, because, even if she moves too sluggishly to halt suddenly, she is preferable to no one. However, she is ill and unable to attend. Timothy is also seated there, coughing and voicing grievances. For ten years he has been in the process of dying, and for another ten years he will continue dying. That sort cannot even perish and complete the matter . . . they are incapable of adhering to anything, including illness, for a sufficient duration to conclude it. They are a dreadfully irresponsible family and I am unaware of what will happen to them, though maybe Providence knows.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0001 }

Mrs. Sowerby uttered a sigh, seemingly somewhat skeptical about how much Providence actually knew regarding the matter.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0002 }

“On Tuesday, Thirza went in concerning her eyes once more, didn't she? How did the specialist assess them?” she went on.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0003 }

“He was very happy,” Nell remarked cheerfully. “He mentions that they have improved significantly and he believes she is no longer at risk of going entirely blind. However, he notes that she will not ever be capable of reading extensively or performing detailed needlework in the future. In what manner are the arrangements for your bazaar progressing?”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0004 }

Arrangements for a supper and fair were being made by the Ladies’ Aid Society, with Mrs. Sowerby acting as the leader and driving force behind the project.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0005 }

“Fairly good . . . which brings something to mind. Mrs. Wace believes it would be lovely to arrange a booth resembling a kitchen from former days and offer a meal consisting of baked beans, doughnuts, pie, and similar items. Old-style decorations are being gathered by us from all over. The braided rugs belonging to her mother will be lent to us by Mrs. Simon Fletcher, a few aged chairs by Mrs. Levi Gammon, and her cupboard featuring glass doors will be lent to us by Aunt Mary Shaw. Thirza will allow us to use her brass candlesticks, I imagine? Furthermore, every piece of old tableware we can obtain is desired by us. Having an authentic blue willow ware platter is something Mrs. Wace particularly insists upon if one can be located by us. Yet one does not appear to be owned by anyone. Are you aware of a place where one might be acquired by us?”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0006 }

“Miss Lavinia Pembroke possesses one, so I will draft a letter inquiring whether she would be willing to lend it for the event,” Nell remarked.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0007 }

“Indeed, my hope is that you will. My expectation is that the supper will occur in approximately two weeks. Predictions of rain and tempests around that period are being made by Uncle Zeb Pullen; consequently, fair weather is almost certainly guaranteed for us.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0008 }

It could be noted that the aforementioned “Uncle Zeb” resembled other prophets in one respect, as he received little respect among his own people. Indeed, he was regarded as a perpetual laughingstock because his forecasts concerning the weather were rarely accurate. It was the custom of Mr. Elisha Duckett, a man who possessed the mistaken belief that he was a town humorist, to remark that no resident of Brierley ever considered checking the Port Marlow daily papers to learn the weather forecasts. Instead, they simply inquired of Uncle Zeb what conditions to anticipate the next day and anticipated the exact reverse. Undeterred by this, Uncle Zeb continued to issue his predictions.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0009 }

“We desire to finish the fair prior to the election occurring,” Mrs. Sowerby added, “because the candidates are bound to attend and lavish a great deal of money. The Tories are distributing bribes everywhere, meaning they should be afforded an opportunity to expend their funds honorably for a change.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0010 }

Out of faithfulness to the memory of Obed, Nell held fiery Conservative views, yet she remained silent. Getting Mrs. Sowerby onto the topic of politics was something she knew to avoid. From a municipality in British Columbia, she possessed a letter addressed to Thirza, bearing a postmark.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0011 }

“It likely comes from the uncle of the children,” she declared with excitement upon reaching home. “Oh, Thirza, I am curious about what he writes concerning them.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0012 }

“Opening it to look inside could be the finest idea,” Thirza stated abruptly. An attentive spectator might have suspected that she too felt excitement, yet she preferred death over displaying such emotion.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0013 }

Nell ripped the envelope open and scanned the slightly messy and badly penned text inside.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0014 }

“He states that taking the children this spring is impossible for him . . . he has been ill for the majority of the winter and his wedding has been postponed. He asks whether we are able to hold onto them until the autumn, at which point he will attempt to take them. We shall, naturally, will we not Thirza?”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0015 }

“I fail to see any other option open to us,” Thirza remarked with a somewhat stern expression, even as a hidden sense of ease came over her. “In any case, they do not cause as much difficulty as before . . . or perhaps we have simply grown accustomed to them. Robin’s behavior is much better than it was.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0016 }

“His behavior has undoubtedly improved,” Nell remarked guardedly, as though she hesitated to offer a similar endorsement regarding his character.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0017 }

When Nell arrived home from school the evening before, she discovered that Thirza was out attending an Aid meeting, Lucy was sleeping on the sofa in the kitchen, and Robin was inside the sitting room closet, happily consuming what was in a jar of Thirza’s well-known yellow plum preserves . . . “company jam,” as Robin termed it . . . which he was prohibited from touching. A very guilty expression crossed his face as Nell swooped down on him and pulled him quickly from the closet.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0018 }

“Robin Farrow, do you not realize how terribly wrong it is for you to be consuming that jam, given that you received instructions to never tamper with a single item inside that closet?”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0019 }

“Indeed, I was aware that it wasn't right,” Robin acknowledged with discomfort, “nevertheless, plum jam tastes terribly good, Nell. My intention was merely to look inside, and its appearance was so inviting that I decided to have only a tiny sample. I dipped my finger inside . . .” Nell uttered a groan . . . “and licked every bit off. Because the taste surpassed my wildest expectations, I grabbed a spoon and simply went to town.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0020 }

Nell delivered a sermon so grave regarding the wickedness of taking plum jam that Robin was filled with remorse and swore through penitent kisses that he would not repeat the act.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0021 }

“At least there is going to be an abundance of preserve in paradise, which provides some consolation,” he remarked contentedly.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0022 }

Nell suppressed a smile before it could form.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0023 }

“Maybe there will be . . . should we desire it,” she remarked, “However, why do you believe that?”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0024 }

“Why, the catechism contains it,” Robin said.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0025 }

“Oh, no, the catechism contains nothing of that sort, Robin.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0026 }

“But I tell you there is,” Robin insisted. “That question Thirza taught me last Sunday had it. ‘Why should we love God?’ The answer is, ‘Because He makes preserves, and redeems us.’ Jam is just called preserves in a holy way.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0027 }

“I must get a drink of water,” said Nell hastily. Returning later, she spent considerable effort and time making Robin understand that the meaning of the mentioned catechism question was altered significantly by a particular comma.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0028 }

“Well, I figured it was just too good to be real,” he finally uttered, giving a sigh filled with let-down certainty. “And what’s more, I couldn’t figure out when He’d get around to making jam if it’s an uninterrupted Sabbath day, like it says in the hymn. I doubt I even desire to go to heaven. Will there never be a single Saturday in heaven, Nell?”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0029 }

“Yes, Saturdays, and all manner of other lovely days. Furthermore, Robin, each day in heaven will surpass the previous one in beauty,” Nell comforted him, feeling somewhat relieved that Thirza was absent and thus spared from being scandalized. It goes without saying that Thirza was rearing the twins according to traditional religious doctrines and forbade any imaginative theorizing about such matters. Every Sunday, Robin and Lucy were instructed to memorize two verses from the Bible, a catechism query, and a hymn. Lucy absorbed her lessons submissively and repeated them like a small automaton, possessing about the same degree of comprehension or engagement as if she actually were a device. Robin, by contrast, possessed an active inquisitiveness, regularly posing queries that caused Thirza to shudder regarding his ultimate destiny.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0030 }

“Chester Mott says our sole activity in heaven will be strolling about in white dresses while playing harps; additionally, he expresses a wish to delay going there until he reaches old age, thinking he might find it more appealing at that time. He also believes wearing dresses will be awful, a sentiment I share. What reason prevents male angels from wearing trousers, Nell? Chester Mott pays attention to such matters because he is destined to become a minister. Becoming a minister is mandatory for him since his grandmother bequeathed funds for his college education on the strict condition that he enters the ministry. In her view, having a minister in the family was extremely ‘spectable. Chester remarks that he isn't overly bothered . . . even though he would prefer being a blacksmith . . . yet he is determined to enjoy himself as much as possible prior to entering the ministry, as he anticipates very little enjoyment later. Being a minister is not my plan. My intention is to become a shopkeeper, similar to Mr. Blair, and stock huge quantities of candy and bananas. However, I would quite enjoy attending your version of heaven if I were permitted to play a mouth organ rather than a harp. Do you think they would allow it?”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0031 }

“Indeed, I believe they’d do so if that were your desire,” was the sole response Nell felt able to utter.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0032 }

That night, the B.V.I.S. convened at the home of Mr. Gorham Pullen, every member having been urged to come because there was significant business to deliberate upon. The B.V.I.S. was thriving, having achieved remarkable results already. When the spring was young, Mr. Major Tranter had fulfilled his pledge by clearing the stumps, leveling the ground, and sowing grass seed along his entire farm frontage. Inspired either by a resolve not to be outdone by a Tranter or driven to act by Improvers within their own families, twelve other men had duplicated his efforts. Consequently, expansive stretches of fine, soft grass now occupied the places where ugly bushes or thickets had previously grown. In comparison, the untouched farm fronts appeared so terrible that those who owned them were quietly embarrassed into deciding to try their hand at improvements the following spring. Furthermore, the triangular patch of land where the roads intersected had been cleared of debris and sown with grass, and the geranium bed planted by Nell, remaining untouched by any roaming cow, had already been positioned right in the middle.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0033 }

On the whole, those in the Improvement Society believed their progress was splendid, despite Mr. Levi Gammon, who was discreetly petitioned by a chosen delegation concerning the ancient dwelling on his higher property, flatly informing them that he would not permit them to tamper with it.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0034 }

During this particular gathering, they planned to draft a petition to the school trustees, respectfully requesting the erection of a fence around the schoolyard; moreover, they were to deliberate a proposal for setting out several decorative trees near the church, provided the society’s money would allow for it . . . because, as Nell remarked, beginning a new subscription was pointless while the hall stayed blue. The members had gathered in the Pullens’ parlor, and Odette was already standing to propose that a committee be named to ascertain and report back regarding the cost of the aforementioned trees, when Tibby Tulk burst in, outfitted in a pompadour and frills to the absolute limit. Tibby was accustomed to arriving late . . . “in order to render her arrival more striking,” malicious individuals claimed. Tibby’s arrival on this occasion was undeniably striking, as she stopped theatricality in the center of the room, raised her hands, rolled her eyes, and cried out, “I’ve just heard something perfectly awful. What do you think? Mr. Judson Tibbs is going to rent all the road fence of his farm to a patent medicine company to paint advertisements on.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0035 }

For a single moment in her existence, Tibby Tulk produced the exact stir she wished for. Had she hurled an explosive amidst the self-satisfied Improvers, her impact could scarcely have been greater.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0036 }

“That is impossible,” Nell uttered expressionlessly.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0037 }

“When I first heard it, that’s precisely what I uttered, don’t you know,” remarked Tibby, who was deriving immense enjoyment from herself. “I expressed that it wasn't possible for it to be true . . . that Judson Tibbs lacked the heart for such an act, don’t you know. However, father encountered him this afternoon, inquiring about the matter, and he confirmed it WAS true. Imagine that! The Stonebridge road runs side-on to his farm, and viewing advertisements for pills and plasters stretched all along it will appear so completely dreadful, don’t you know?”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0038 }

The Improvers were indeed fully aware. The most uninspired person in the group was able to visualize the bizarre appearance of a half-mile wooden fence covered in those notices. Any consideration regarding the grounds of the church and school disappeared in the face of this sudden threat. Rules of order and guidelines were discarded, and Nell, feeling hopeless, abandoned her attempt to record the minutes altogether. Everyone spoke simultaneously, creating a terrible uproar.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0039 }

“Oh, we must remain composed,” begged Nell, despite being the one experiencing the greatest agitation among the group, “and attempt to devise a method to stop him.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0040 }

“I fail to see how you will stop him,” Odette declared with bitterness. “Judson Tibbs’s reputation is well known to all. For financial gain, he would commit any act. He possesses no public spirit whatsoever, nor does he have any appreciation for beauty.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0041 }

The outlook appeared fairly discouraging. Because Judson Tibbs and his sister constituted the sole Parkers residing in Brierley, family ties offered no possibility of influence. Being a woman of indisputably advanced years, Martha Tibbs looked with disfavor upon youth as a whole and the Improvers especially. As for Judson, he was a cheerful, suave individual whose disposition was so consistently pleasant and mild that his scarcity of comrades seemed astonishing. It was possible that he had emerged victorious from an excessive number of commercial dealings. . . a habit that rarely engenders widespread affection. People considered him to be exceedingly “sharp” and held the prevailing view that he “hadn’t much principle.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0042 }

“He will always seize an opportunity to ‘turn an honest penny,’ as he puts it,” Gideon Duckett stated regarding Judson Tibbs.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0043 }

“Does anyone possess any influence with him?” Nell inquired in despair.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0044 }

“He pays a visit to Louisa Tranter at Pale Sands,” Carrie Mott put forward. “She might be able to persuade him against letting out his fences.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0045 }

“Not that woman,” Hugh stated with force. “Louisa Tranter is someone I am well acquainted with. While Village Improvement Societies aren't something she ‘believes’ in, dollars and cents certainly are. It is far more probable that she would push Judson forward instead of talking him out of it.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0046 }

“Appointing a delegation to go to him and object is our sole option,” Julia Bell stated, “and sending girls is necessary, as his politeness toward boys is doubtful . . . yet I refuse to go, meaning any nomination for me is pointless.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0047 }

“It would be best for Nell to go by herself,” remarked Oliver Mott. “If anyone is capable of persuading Judson, it’s her.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0048 }

Nell made an objection. She was ready to travel and handle the speaking, though she insisted that companions accompany her “for moral support.” Consequently, Isolde and Odette were chosen to offer her moral backing, after which the Improvers disbanded, humming with resentment like furious bees. Nell felt so anxious that she failed to fall asleep until close to dawn, whereupon she envisioned in a dream that the trustees had enclosed the school with a fence and inscribed “Try Purple Pills” across its entire surface.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0049 }

The following afternoon, Judson Tibbs received a visit from the committee. Nell made an eloquent plea opposing his wicked plan, with Odette and Isolde offering her brave, moral backing. Judson remained smooth, polished, and complimentary; offered them a few compliments as delicate as sunflowers; expressed genuine regret at turning down such delightful young women . . . yet business remained business; he was unable to permit sentiment to interfere during these difficult times.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0050 }

“However, I am going to share what my actions will be,” he stated, his pale, prominent eyes gleaming with a sparkle. “I am going to instruct the agent to employ exclusively attractive, appealing shades . . . yellow and red and similar ones. I am going to instruct him that under no circumstances is he permitted to paint the advertisements blue.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0051 }

The defeated committee withdrew, holding thoughts forbidden to be spoken.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0052 }

“There is nothing more within our power, so we have to place our faith in Providence for whatever remains,” Odette remarked, mirroring Mrs. Sowerby’s expression and delivery without realizing it.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0053 }

“I wonder whether Mr. Wace might be able to help,” pondered Isolde.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0054 }

Nell gave a shake of her head.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0055 }

“No, troubling Mr. Wace is pointless, particularly at this moment with the baby being this ill. Judson would evade him just as effortlessly as he does us, even though he has commenced attending church rather consistently at present. The sole reason for that is that Louisa Tranter’s father holds the position of elder and is extremely strict regarding those matters.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0056 }

“Only Judson Tibbs in all of Brierley would ever think to lease out his fences,” Odette declared, filled with indignation. “As stingy as Levi Gammon or Lorenzo White are, even they would not degrade themselves like that. Public opinion would mean too much to them.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0057 }

When the details emerged, popular sentiment undoubtedly turned against Judson Tibbs, yet that provided little relief. Judson laughed inwardly and stood his ground, leaving the Improvers attempting to accept the likely sight of commercial signs ruining the most beautiful section of the Stonebridge road, until Nell calmly stood up at the subsequent Society gathering when the leader requested committee updates, declaring that Mr. Judson Tibbs had directed her to tell the Society he would refrain from leasing his fencing to the Patent Medicine Company.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0058 }

Odette and Isolde gazed as though they could scarcely trust what they were hearing. Although the normally rigorous rules of parliamentary etiquette within the B.V.I.S. prevented them from immediately expressing their inquisitiveness, Nell was overwhelmed with demands for an explanation once the meeting of the Society came to a close. Nell, however, possessed no explanation that she could offer. Judson Tibbs had caught up to her along the road the previous night, informing her of his choice to indulge the B.V.I.S. regarding its strange bias against advertisements for patent medicine. Then and throughout all the time that followed, that was the extent of what Nell would state, and it was nothing less than the plain truth; nevertheless, as Odette Pullen walked home and shared with Oliver Mott her deep conviction that something further lay beneath the enigmatic shift in Judson Tibbs’s attitude than Nell Harcourt had disclosed, she was likewise speaking the truth.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0059 }

The previous evening, Nell had visited old Mrs. Stanhope’s along the shore road, returning home via a shortcut that took her across the low shore fields before passing through the beech wood under Robert Dickson’s, following a narrow footpath that emerged onto the main road right above the Lake of Glassy Waters . . . which ordinary people called Pembroke’s pond.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0060 }

Right where the trail began, a pair of men sat in their buggies, pulled over to the road's edge. Judson Tibbs was one; Tobias Corcoran was the other, a man from Stonebridge against whom nothing dishonorable had ever been proven, as Mrs. Sowerby would have informed you in vivid italics. He sold farm machinery on commission and held a notable position in political affairs. In every political pie that was baked, he had a finger . . . certain folks claimed all his fingers . . .; and since a general election was imminent in Canada, Tobias Corcoran had spent many weeks as a occupied man, traveling through the county to gather support for the candidate of his party. Exactly when Nell stepped out from beneath the overhanging branches of the beech, she caught Corcoran saying, “If you’ll vote for Amesbury, Tibbs . . . well, I’ve a note for that pair of harrows you’ve got in the spring. I suppose you wouldn’t object to having it back, eh?”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0061 }

“We . . . ll, seeing as you express it like that,” Judson drawled, grinning, “I suppose I may as well comply. In these difficult times, an individual has to safeguard his personal affairs.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0062 }

At that exact second, Nell was spotted by the two of them, causing their talk to stop suddenly. Giving a cold bow, Nell continued walking, her chin held just a bit higher than normal. Shortly afterward, she was caught up to by Judson Tibbs.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0063 }

“Need a ride, Nell?” he asked in a friendly manner.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0064 }

“I am obliged, but no,” replied Nell courteously, yet her tone possessed a sharp, penetrating scorn that penetrated even the thick skin of Judson Tibbs. His cheeks flushed crimson and he gave his reins an irritated jerk; however, self-preservation halted him in the very next instant. With an anxious gaze, he observed Nell continuing her firm progression, her eyes fixed straight ahead without turning to either side. Was she aware of Corcoran’s explicit proposition and the overly clear manner in which he himself had agreed to it? A curse on Corcoran! Should he fail to express his intentions in safer language, he was bound to find himself in difficulty before long. Furthermore, a curse on red-haired female teachers who possessed a tendency to suddenly appear from beech forests where they had no right to be located. Supposing Nell had overheard, Judson Tibbs—evaluating her character by his own base standards, as the local proverb expressed it, and consequently deceiving himself, as individuals of his sort typically do—was convinced that she would spread the news everywhere. At this point, Judson Tibbs, as previously demonstrated, cared little for the community's judgment; nevertheless, being exposed for taking a bribe would prove disastrous; moreover, should the story ever come to the attention of Isaac Tranter, all prospects of securing Louisa Odette, along with her attractive financial future as the daughter of a prosperous farmer, would be permanently destroyed. Judson Tibbs was aware that Mr. Tranter already viewed him with a degree of suspicion; he was in no position to chance anything.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0065 }

“Ahem . . . I was hoping to speak with you regarding the small issue we talked about a few days ago, Nell. My decision now is that I will not lease my fences to that firm. An organization whose goal matches yours deserves support.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0066 }

Nell unbent to the slightest possible degree.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0067 }

“I am grateful,” she remarked.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0068 }

“And . . . and . . . there is no need to speak of that brief chat I had with Tobias.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0069 }

“Under no circumstances do I intend to speak of it,” Nell stated coldly, since she would have preferred to behold all the fences in Brierley covered in ads rather than lower herself to strike a deal with a person willing to trade his vote.
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0070 }

“Precisely . . . precisely,” concurred Judson, believing that they held a wonderful mutual understanding. “I did not expect you would. Naturally, I was merely teasing Tobias . . . he believes he is so terribly clever and sharp. I do not intend to vote for Amesbury. I shall vote for Hollis just as I have ever done . . . you will observe that when the election takes place. I simply egged Tobias on to discover if he would declare himself. And regarding the fence, everything is fine . . . you may inform the Improvers of that.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0071 }

“A world requires every type of person, according to what I’ve frequently heard, yet I believe a few might be done without,” Nell remarked to her image in the east gable mirror later that evening. “My conscience remains untroubled regarding that matter, as I would not have spoken of the shameful occurrence to anyone regardless. Who or what deserves gratitude for this is beyond my understanding. It was not brought about by any action of mine, and accepting that Providence operates through the sort of politics practiced by men such as Judson Tibbs and Tobias Corcoran is difficult.”
{: #nw-v02-c14-p0072 }
